example.answer: It takes about 10.24 years for the money to double.
example.problem: Money grows at 7% per year. How many years does it take to double? Solve 1.07^t = 2.
steps: Take the natural log of both sides: t × ln(1.07) = ln(2).
example.title: How long to double your money

faqs.a: On most calculators, log means base 10 and ln means base e (≈ 2.71828). They answer the same question — 'to what power?' — for different bases.
faqs.q: What is the difference between log and ln?

faqs.a: The number e is the base of continuous growth: e^x is the unique function that is its own slope. That makes natural logs the default in calculus, physics and finance.
faqs.q: Why is the number e special?

formula.expr: log₁₀(x): 10 to what power equals x?
formula.label: Common logarithm

howItWorks: A logarithm answers one question: a base raised to what power gives my number? The common logarithm (log₁₀) counts powers of 10, so log₁₀(1000) = 3 because 10³ = 1000. The natural logarithm (ln) counts powers of e, the mathematical constant ≈ 2.71828 that describes continuous growth. For any other base, the calculator uses the change-of-base formula, which rewrites the problem as a division of two natural logs.

Logarithms are only defined for positive numbers and positive bases other than 1. That is not an arbitrary rule: a positive base raised to any power is always positive, so no power can ever produce zero or a negative number — and 1 raised to any power is always 1, so base 1 could never pin down an answer.
intro: Work out common logarithms (base 10), natural logarithms (base e), or a logarithm in any base you choose. Type your number and see the answer with every step shown.

mistakes.text: A logarithm asks 'b to what power gives x?', and a positive base raised to any power is always positive. So log(0) and log of a negative number do not exist.
mistakes.title: Taking the log of zero or a negative number

mistakes.text: Any positive base raised to 0 is 1, so log_b(1) = 0 for every valid base. The input 1 is not special — its logarithm is.
mistakes.title: Thinking log(1) is 1

mistakes.text: 1^y is always 1, so base 1 can never equal anything else. The calculator rejects it instead of guessing.
mistakes.title: Using base 1

mistakes.text: Logarithms turn multiplication into addition: log(x × y) = log(x) + log(y). But log(x + y) is not log(x) + log(y) — there is no shortcut for a sum inside a log.
mistakes.title: Confusing log(x + y) with log(x) + log(y)
